issues.description: The problem statement and UML refer to a class named 'Stock' (and instruct students to modify/use it), but the template repository provides an 'Inventory' class that implements the stock functionality while Stock.java is empty. The solution also uses Inventory (SealSaloon.stock is of type Inventory). This name/type mismatch (Stock vs Inventory) is a structural inconsistency that will confuse students about which class to implement or use and where to put the stock-related methods.
issues.suggestedFix: Make the type/name consistent across artifacts. Either (A) update the problem statement and UML to refer to 'Inventory' instead of 'Stock', or (B) provide a proper Stock class implementation in the template (or rename Inventory to Stock) so that the template, UML, and solution use the same class name and type for the shared stock. Ensure method signatures and usages match the chosen name.

issues.description: The problem statement and UML describe a Stock class as the central inventory type, but the provided template and the solution use a class named Inventory for the same conceptual entity (and template contains an empty Stock.java). This mismatch (Stock vs Inventory) creates a mapping barrier: students reading the problem expect to find/modify a Stock class but instead must work with Inventory or an empty Stock file. It is unclear whether students should implement Stock or use Inventory, which adds unnecessary cognitive load and may lead to implementing the wrong file or renaming classes incorrectly.
issues.suggestedFix: Unify the identifier across artifacts. Either rename the Inventory class/file to Stock (and update all references in template and solution to use Stock), or update the problem statement and UML to refer to Inventory instead of Stock. Also remove or populate the empty template Stock.java so students are not misled by an unused file.
